BITC: A rotation strategy that moves between bitcoin futures and US Treasury securities following a trend signal based on bitcoin's price momentum. When bitcoin's trend is up it holds bitcoin futures, and when the trend turns down it shelters in Treasuries.
LOPP: US companies that pass Gabelli's sustainability guidelines, mostly industrial firms working in energy, water, waste and efficient equipment. It blends environmental goals with old-economy businesses, so it looks more like a factory and utility portfolio than a solar fund.
TPLS: A core-plus bond portfolio: Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt at the center, with room for up to a quarter in lower-rated junk bonds for extra yield. The plus sleeve lifts income while adding credit risk to a mainly high-quality base.
MYMI: Municipal bonds maturing in 2029 from states, schools and local agencies across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. It suits money with a known 2029 purpose, and prices settle down as the maturity year approaches.
SNPG: Growth companies from the S&P 500, screened and scored so each industry favors firms with stronger environmental, social and governance records than their peers. It keeps the shape of a standard growth fund while tilting toward better-rated corporate citizens.
VNSE: A select, concentrated portfolio of mostly mid and large companies chosen by Vaughan Nelson's fundamental research, led by technology, with energy and industry behind. Few holdings means each pick matters, and the managers hold for years rather than trade.
FOWF: Defense companies from the US and its allies working on emerging warfare technology: missiles, aircraft, drones, sensors and cyber defense. Industry takes about three fifths and technology most of the rest, tying the fund to allied military spending.
VBCI: Corporate bonds from big technology, banking and media issuers that mature around 2035, when the fund itself is set to end. It works much like a single bond with a target end date: collect interest, then principal comes back as bonds mature.
NTRL: A market neutral event strategy: long and short positions in companies caught up in announced mergers and other big corporate events, balanced so market direction matters little. It aims for steady, deal-driven returns, with losses when deals fall apart or spreads widen.
JANJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
FTAG: Agriculture companies worldwide: seed and crop chemical giants, fertilizer makers and farm machinery firms, with materials producers over half the fund. It is a bet on farm spending and crop prices, driven by weather, harvests and food demand.
JCHI: Actively managed Chinese companies across mainland, Hong Kong and US listings, led by internet platforms and banks. JPMorgan's managers pick across China's share classes in one portfolio, carrying the region's regulatory and currency risks.
LTCC: Direct ownership of Litecoin, a long-running cryptocurrency designed as a faster, lighter alternative to bitcoin, held as the fund's only asset. It moves with crypto sentiment generally and Litecoin's own adoption, and sharp daily swings are normal.
GDOG: Direct ownership of Dogecoin, the meme-born cryptocurrency featuring a Shiba Inu dog, held as the fund's only asset. Its price is driven mostly by online enthusiasm and celebrity attention, making it among the most speculative assets in any brokerage account.
HBRD: Hybrid corporate debt: subordinated bonds that sit between regular bonds and preferred stock in a company's pecking order, issued in US dollars. Hybrids pay more than senior bonds for the extra risk, a middle path between bond safety and stock-like returns.
LTTI: Long-term US Treasury bonds, those maturing in more than 20 years, combined with options on a long Treasury fund to generate target income. Long Treasuries swing hard when rates move, and the option overlay adds payouts without removing that rate risk.
FLXI: An actively managed multisector bond portfolio that can roam across corporate, government, mortgage and other debt types as Invesco's managers see value. That freedom means its risk profile shifts over time, unlike a fixed core bond index fund.
CGOV: Treasury bills maturing within three months, the shortest and safest US government debt. It is a cash alternative for parking money, earning a small interest trickle while keeping the value about as steady as a bank account.
BRKW: Leveraged weekly exposure to Berkshire Hathaway's class B shares through swaps and stock, plus weekly cash distributions. It turns a famously steady conglomerate into something far jumpier with leverage, and the payouts come from the structure rather than from dividends.
TINY: Nanotechnology companies: firms working at the scale of atoms and molecules, from chip-making equipment and precision instruments to advanced materials. It is a niche science theme spread across technology, health care and materials, with many small, research-heavy names.
NERD: Video game companies worldwide: publishers, console makers, mobile game firms and the platforms where games are sold and streamed. It is a pure entertainment growth bet whose fortunes follow game releases, player spending and hit titles.
HVAC: Companies that heat, cool and build: air conditioning giants, cooling specialists for data centers, contractors and industrial suppliers. It rides construction spending and the enormous cooling needs of AI data centers, making climate control a growth theme.
IMTG: Mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by US government agencies, pooling home loans of many maturities into interest-paying bonds. It offers steadier income than corporate debt, with returns shaped by how fast homeowners refinance when rates fall.
SHRD: Core bonds, mostly US Treasuries and agency securities, in an index screened to align with Catholic values. It targets plain investment grade income for faith-based investors, and the screen removes issuers whose business conflicts with Catholic teaching.
BMED: Health innovation companies: drug developers, gene and cell therapy firms, diagnostics and life-science toolmakers, picked actively worldwide. It is a growth bet on medical breakthroughs, so trial results and regulators' decisions can swing it sharply.
QTOC: Options on the Nasdaq-100 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each October. It is a leveraged-style bet on big tech rising, with no cushion when the index falls.
FPAS: Short-term debt issued or guaranteed by the US government and its agencies, kept brief in maturity to protect capital. It pays modest interest with very small price swings, suiting money that must be there when needed.
TOCT: Options on the S&P 500 structured for defined protection over a two-year period ending in October 2027, taking gains up to a cap while aiming to shield against losses. The two-year horizon is the trade-off for that level of protection.
JULJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
LQID: Ultra-short bonds and cash-like funds, Treasury bills, short bond funds and top-rated loan funds, plus an options strategy on bonds to add income. It aims to beat money market returns slightly, taking a small step up in risk for extra yield.
DTRE: Property companies behind disruptive technology: data center landlords, cell tower owners and e-commerce warehouse operators, worldwide. It collects rent from the physical backbone of the internet, so it behaves like a property fund with a tech accent.
MUNB: A ladder of tax-exempt municipal bonds maturing in the years running up to 2035, paying out as each rung comes due. It is designed to fund a future goal around 2035 with federal tax-free income along the way.
EUM: A daily inverse bet on emerging market stocks, designed to rise when developing-country shares fall. It resets daily, making it a short-term hedge or trade, and it bleeds value steadily whenever emerging markets trend upward.
MKAM: A simple two-part mix: about half in an S&P 500 fund and about half in Treasury bills maturing within three months, adjusted to soften drawdowns. Half the money always sits in cash-like safety, so it trails in bull markets and cushions bear ones.
DDTM: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each March, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
MFMO: US stocks with the strongest price momentum, picked by a Motley Fool index that favors recent winners, led by chip and technology names. Momentum strategies ride trends well but can crash when leadership flips, since yesterday's winners fall hardest.
BABO: An options income strategy on a single stock, Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce and cloud giant, using contracts tied to its US-listed shares. It pays high distributions from Alibaba's volatility, with gains capped and China-related risks fully in play.
HIYY: An options income strategy on a single stock, Hims and Hers Health, the telehealth company known for hair, skin and weight-loss treatments. It converts a young, volatile stock's swings into distributions, with gains capped and sharp drops largely unprotected.
BITY: Bitcoin exposure through a spot bitcoin fund and futures, paired with options meant to add about two percent in extra monthly income. The options target steadier payouts than bitcoin alone, though bitcoin's price still dominates the result.
PRAE: Global stock funds covering value, small companies and international markets, plus an alternatives overlay of futures, commodities and currencies. The overlay is meant to diversify the stock exposure and soften drops, adding complexity most plain portfolios skip.
CPRA: Options on a Russell 2000 fund structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in April, while taking part in small-cap gains up to a cap. It trades away the strongest small-stock rallies for a softer landing in downturns.
EMIF: Infrastructure in emerging markets: airport operators, water and power utilities and energy transport companies across Latin America, Asia and the Middle East. It collects tolls, fares and utility bills from growing economies, with political and currency risk attached.
CRXP: A core-plus bond portfolio built on mortgage bonds, including agency pools and non-agency home loan trusts, plus corporate and other debt. The plus reach into non-agency mortgages lifts income above plain core funds, with more credit complexity underneath.
KBFR: Small US companies across health care, finance, technology and industry, paired with options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It aims for small-cap growth with a managed cushion, giving up some upside to pay for the protection.
SDCP: Short-term bonds, mostly investment grade US corporate, government and asset-backed debt kept within one to three years of maturity. It emphasizes low volatility income, a step up from cash for money that still needs to stay fairly steady.
TEMX: Growth companies in emerging markets excluding China and Hong Kong, led by Taiwanese and Korean chip giants, with Indian finance and Latin American e-commerce behind. Skipping China sets it apart from standard emerging market funds and concentrates it in Asia's tech exporters.
UXAP: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to accelerate gains without an upside cap over a one-year period ending each April. It is built for strong bull markets, and it carries full exposure to losses when the market falls instead.
EVNT: An event-driven long and short portfolio: stocks of companies facing mergers, spinoffs and other corporate changes, mostly held long with some shorts. It aims for returns driven by deal outcomes rather than market direction, and botched deals are the main hazard.
DUKQ: A tactical rotation among US stock funds of different sizes and styles, from large growth to small value, moving to cash when trends weaken. The manager's timing calls drive results, which can help in downturns and hurt in fast rebounds.
ERET: Property companies and trusts in developed markets screened for stronger environmental performance, from warehouse and health care landlords to data centers. It tilts a global real estate portfolio toward greener buildings and operators, without leaving the property sector.
